title.narrative: Empowerment of Ugandan Youth Networks and Organizations for Youth-Led Gender-responsive Climate Actions, Research and Development

description.narrative:
The Youth Committee of the Uganda National Commission for UNESCO (UNATCOM) established in 2010, has been concerned about the low level of awareness of the youth of Uganda about UNESCO and its programmes designed to empower the youth. Disappointingly, the level of knowledge is not only very low, but even of all the various youth organizations that exist countrywide, only two are associated with UNESCO. These two are UNESCO clubs, one in Gulu University, an upcountry city location and the second at Nakawa Vocational Training College, in Kampala Metropolitan City. This number is too low compared to the situation in the other East African countries such as Rwanda which has 35 UNESCO Clubs and Kenya with 168 UNESCO Clubs and Associations. This is despite the fact that there are many concerns affecting Ugandan youth to address relating to 38.5% of young people aged 10-19 that live in the poorest wealth quintiles, 80% of Uganda’s youth that living in rural areas and one out of four young people aged 10-24 years residing in urban areas have no means for self-empowerment, 19.6% of young people aged 10-19 years living in households where the head of household has no education, 22% of adolescents aged 13-18 years dropping out of school while 8.8 million young people aged 15-24 years not engaged in education, employment or under any training1. Though a National Youth Council Act, 1993 exists, it specifically provides for a National Youth Council which is largely political with no stated focus on the social challenges faced by the youth. There is Uganda Youth Network (UYONET) that purports to be a leading national youth organization working to mainstream young peoples’ engagement in development and governance processes in Uganda and East Africa. This network started in 2002 to respond to the increasing demand for a collective platform for research, training and policy advocacy for young people by young people. However, it does not address the concerns of interest to UNESCO. Statistics indicate that the youth in Uganda have continued to face multitudes of problems namely: Teenage pregnancy (25% of teenage girls in Uganda age 15-19 have had a child or are pregnant), Health risk behaviors (22% of adolescents have ever had sexual intercourse and 10% of sexually active adolescents aged 15-19 years had their first sexual encounter before age 15), Child Marriage (10% of women aged 20-24 years married by age 15), Gender-Based Violence ( 60% of adolescents 10-19 years have experienced physical violence, 42% emotional violence and 10% sexual violence), HIV/AIDS (Every year 9,600 young people aged 15- 19 years are newly infected with HIV)2. A Cross Sectional Survey Study conducted by scholars show that alcohol, substance use and psychosocial competence of adolescents in selected Secondary Schools in Uganda was at 70% 3.

3. Abbo, C, Okello, E.S., Muhwezi, W., Grace Akello, G. and Ovuga, E, (2016): Alcohol, Substance Use and Psychosocial Competence of Adolescents in Selected Secondary Schools in Uganda: A Cross Sectional Survey, Int Neuropsychiatr Dis J. 2016; 7(2): 25387. doi: 10.9734/INDJ/2016/25387
